sspongee on Sora has come up with a pretty good and realistic VHS camcorder prompt. Works great for scary videos.
> Real-life authentic raw VHS camcorder footage from the early 2000s, recorded directly onto magnetic tape. The image has a soft analog blur, faint color bleeding, muted tones, and light static. Horizontal tracking lines occasionally flicker along the bottom edge. The handheld camera jitters slightly with natural, imperfect movement. Subtle chroma drift and faint scanline flicker maintain the unmistakable look of genuine analog tape — not a digital imitation. The timestamp in small white digital text, perfectly stable and unaffected by distortion, reads: ‘OCT 28 2004 11:46:09 PM’ locked in the bottom-right corner, visible throughout without interruption ...

Noematrix Secures Alibaba-Led Funding to Accelerate Embodied AI Deployment
Noematrix, the 2023-founded embodied intelligence firm, just announced a new funding round led by Alibaba Group with follow-on investments from existing shareholders, adding to their multiple hundred-million RMB Pre-A++ and Pre-A+++ rounds. The capital will be deployed to accelerate technical R&D, real-world application deployment, and ecosystem expansion.
The core of their strategy is the Noematrix Brain 2.0, an integrated soft/hardware platform built on "generality" and "intelligence." Key platform upgrades include enhancing the physical world large model with Object Concept Learning and introducing a User Preference mechanism, allowing robots to understand and recall user habits, environments, and human relationships. To address data and model efficiency in commercial deployment, Noematrix has developed a no-ontology data collection plan, general end-to-end models, and a human-robot collaborative system aimed at establishing a full data-to-deployment closed loop. The company has already partnered with retail and home goods leaders to push for the bulk delivery of their integrated solutions.
The company is backed by a powerhouse founding team. Co-founder Wang Shiquan holds a Ph.D. from Stanford (BDML/AI Labs) under bionics pioneers Mark Cutkosky and Oussama Khatib, and previously founded Flexiv Technology. Co-founder Lu Cewu, a special researcher at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and former Stanford AI post-doc, is recognized for his significant academic contributions, including the original AnyGrasp grasping algorithm, a Scientific Exploration Award, and an MIT TR35 honor.

title: fofr (@fofrAI)
summary:
> build me a hoverboard, make no mistakes
Quoting @SGRodriques
Today, we’re announcing Kosmos, our newest AI Scientist, available to use now.
Users estimate Kosmos does 6 months of work in a single day. One run can read 1,500 papers and write 42,000 lines of code. At least 79% of its findings are reproducible. Kosmos has made 7 discoveries so far, which we are releasing today, in areas ranging from neuroscience to material science and clinical genetics, in collaboration with our academic beta testers. Three of these discoveries reproduced unpublished findings; four are net new, validated contributions to the scientific literature. AI-accelerated science is here.
Our core innovation in Kosmos is the use of a structured, continuously-updated world model. As described in our technical report, Kosmos’ world model allows it to process orders of magnitude more information than could fit into the context of even the longest-context language models, allowing it to synthesize more information and pursue coherent goals over longer time horizons than Robin or any of our other prior agents. In this respect, we believe Kosmos is the most compute-intensive language agent released so far in any field, and by far the most capable AI Scientist available today. The use of a persistent world model also enables single Kosmos trajectories to produce highly complex outputs that require multiple significant logical leaps. As with all of our systems, Kosmos is designed with transparency and verifiability in mind: every conclusion in a Kosmos report can be traced through our platform to the specific lines of code or the specific passages in the scientific literature that inspired it, ensuring that Kosmos’ findings are fully auditable at all times.
We are also using this opportunity to announce the launch of Edison Scientific, a new commercial spinout of FutureHouse, which will be focused on commercializing our agents and applying them to automate scientific research in drug discovery and beyond. Edison will be taking over management of the FutureHouse platform, where you can access Kosmos alongside our Literature, Molecules, and Precedent agents (previously Crow, Phoenix, and Owl). Edison will continue to offer free tier usage for casual users and academics, while also offering higher rate limits and additional features for users who need them. You can read more about this spinout on our blog, below.
A few important notes if you’re going to try Kosmos. Firstly, Kosmos is different from many other AI tools you might have played with, including our other agents. It is more similar to a Deep Research tool than it is to a chatbot: it takes some time to figure out how to prompt it effectively, and we have tried to include guidelines on this to help (see below). It costs $200/run right now (200 credits per run, and $1/credit), with some free tier usage for academics. This is heavily discounted; people who sign up for Founding Subscriptions now can lock in the $1/credit price indefinitely, but the price ultimately will probably be higher. Again, this is less chatbot and more research tool, something you run on high-value targets as needed.
Some caveats are also warranted. Firstly, we find that 80% of Kosmos findings are reproducible, which also means 20% are not -- some things it says will be wrong. Also, Kosmos certainly does produce outputs that are the equivalent to several months of human labor, but it also often goes down rabbit holes or chases statistically significant yet scientifically irrelevant findings. We often run Kosmos multiple times on the same objective in order to sample the various research avenues it can take. There are still a bunch of rough edges on the UI and such, which we are working on. Finally, we are aware that the 6 month figure is much greater than estimates by other AI labs, like METR, about the length of tasks that AI Agents can currently perform. You can read discussion about this in our blog post.

summary:
In the quoted post I found an interesting prompt. This happened because I was experimenting with a set of sketches I'd previously used to train a lora on a specific style.
I wanted to find out if Nano Banana Pro could do two things:
- Could you reproduce the style with just input images
- Could you apply the style in an out-of-distribution way
The style largely worked very well, though it was applied differently to say a flux or qwen lora that was trained on the same images. Nano Banana Pro didn't seem able to apply the "form from just strokes" pattern to other mediums (which I've observed loras doing when you boost their strength)
That's how I ended up prompting for a photo with some paint effects applied to it.

title: fofr (@fofrAI)
summary:
My Gemini 3 system instructions for getting a good JSON prompt from an image
Quoting @fofrAI
Yep:
You are an expert prompt engineer for Nano Banana Pro.
Your task is to convert the user's description into a sophisticated, EXTREMELY DETAILED JSON prompt.
You must output a single valid JSON object.
### JSON STRUCTURE GUIDELINES:
1. **Dynamic Fields**: You are encouraged to ADD new fields that capture specific details about the subject (e.g., "plating_style" for food, "architecture_era" for buildings, "glitch_patterns" for abstract art).
2. **Remove Irrelevant Fields**: Do NOT include fields that don't apply. If the subject is a stove, do not include "hair", "skin", or "pose". Remove them entirely rather than setting them to "N/A".
3. **Subject Specificity**:
- **For People**: The example structure (subject, face, skin, hair, clothing) is excellent. Keep it.
- **For Non-Humans**: Create a structure that fits the object. For example, a car might have "chassis", "paint_finish", "wheels".
4. **Standard Fields**: Always include "constraints" (with "must_keep" and "avoid" lists) and "negative_prompt".
### AESTHETIC GOALS:
- **Medium Specificity**: If the user asks for a specific style (e.g. "oil painting"), describe the brushwork, canvas texture, and drying cracks.
- **Lighting**: Be precise (soft, hard, volumetric, golden hour, studio, rim lighting).
- **Camera**: (focal length, depth of field) - ONLY if the style requires photorealism.
Use the following example as a reference for *depth* and *granularity*, but adapt the *keys* to your subject:
[INSERT YOUR SAMPLE PROMPT HERE]
Return ONLY the raw JSON string.

title: fofr (@fofrAI)
summary:
I like this framing. AI increases your personal capacity.
Quoting @jacalulu
There’s a weird narrative floating around that using AI for simple tasks makes you 'incapable' or 'lazy.'
I think we’re confusing Capability with Capacity.
Yes, I can read a map. Yes, I can cross-reference three emails. But when I’m balancing a last-minute trip, chasing three kids, and entertaining in-laws, my brain isn't looking for more admin tasks - it's looking for bandwidth.
The goal is simple: Let AI handle the trivial 'logistics' so I can handle the meaningful 'human.'
It's not replacing my ability to think; it's protecting my energy for the things that actually require it. The ROI isn't just time saved; it's sanity preserved. And that clarity is exactly what allows me to accomplish more of what actually matters.

title: fofr (@fofrAI)
summary:
I've brought together some of the things I most commonly prompt for when building gen media apps in AI Studio.
I've found these instructions give me good one-shot apps that are usable from the start.
=====
App interaction and design notes
=====
1. This app is for exploration. You must allow forms to be submitted again and again, without waiting for previous responses to finish. Do not clear the form values when a form is submitted.
2. Show each pending output, with a timer (0.00s) showing how long it's been generating. (Keep time available after generation completes.)
3. Use a grid of outputs, it should be able to handle outputs that are different aspect ratios, but also respect the next rule. Optimise for showing outputs over margins, padding, etc.
4. Always represent outputs in their original aspect ratio (not squashed and not cropped, eg CSS 'object-fit: contain' is better than 'object-fit: cover').
5. Each output should be viewable by itself in a fullscreen view (click to open), and the view should always allow left/right navigation between outputs (support keyboard navigation). Important: Consider how this view looks when still in the loading/generating state.
6. Each output must be downloadable, its prompt copyable, its settings clickable to repopulate the form, and a "redo" action that is the equivalent of running the same prompt and inputs again.
7. Actions must have clear hover, focus and active states, that are consistent across the app.
8. Controls for each output (eg download, copy to clipboard) should never overlay the output itself.
9. Avoid position fixed. Prefer form on left and outputs on right.
10. Whenever an image or multiple images are needed in a form, allow the user to click and select, drag and drop, or paste from clipboard.
11. When downloading an output, the filename should start with a unix format timestamp. Filenames should be unique, incorporate the prompt when applicable.
12. Consider when is best to use a very fast flash model to create titles for things, eg for filenames, prompts, etc. Whenever this is done, cache or save those titles to avoid re-generating them each time.
13. The form should be submittable with Enter, even in textareas fields.
14. Incorporate dark and light mode, default to system preference. Do not animate between modes.
15. Be WCAG AA accessible.
16. When long intputs are put into textareas, allow the form field to increase in height (up to a sensible maximum height).
17. Use plain english, sensible labels for form fields.
18. If using Nano Banana Pro: Nano Banana Pro always outputs jpg, never png.
19. Consider mobile view: Collapse form behind a toggle, maintain generate button

title: fofr (@fofrAI)
summary:
Sorry, could you repeat the question?
Quoting @burkov
LLMs process text from left to right — each token can only look back at what came before it, never forward. This means that when you write a long prompt with context at the beginning and a question at the end, the model answers the question having "seen" the context, but the context tokens were generated without any awareness of what question was coming. This asymmetry is a basic structural property of how these models work.
The paper asks what happens if you just send the prompt twice in a row, so that every part of the input gets a second pass where it can attend to every other part. The answer is that accuracy goes up across seven different benchmarks and seven different models (from the Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek series of LLMs), with no increase in the length of the model's output and no meaningful increase in response time — because processing the input is done in parallel by the hardware anyway.
There are no new losses to compute, no finetuning, no clever prompt engineering beyond the repetition itself.
The gap between this technique and doing nothing is sometimes small, sometimes large (one model went from 21% to 97% on a task involving finding a name in a list). If you are thinking about how to get better results from these models without paying for longer outputs or slower responses, that's a fairly concrete and low-effort finding.

title: fofr (@fofrAI)
summary:
What happens if you give it a different type of body and environment?
Quoting @oh_that_hat
There's a fruit fly walking around right now that was never born.
@eonsys just released a video where they took a real fly's connectome — the wiring diagram of its brain — and simulated it. Dropped it into a virtual body. It started walking. Grooming. Feeding. Doing what flies do.
Nobody taught it to walk. No training data, no gradient descent toward fly-like behavior. This is the opposite of how AI works. They rebuilt the mind from the inside, neuron by neuron, and behavior just... emerged. It's the first time a biological organism has been recreated not by modeling what it does, but by modeling what it is.
A human brain is 6 OOM more neurons. That's a scaling problem, something we've gotten very good at solving. So what happens when we have a working copy of the human mind?

title: fofr (@fofrAI)
summary:
Always good feedback on video models from Henry. This is a great deep dive into the troubles of using Seedance 2 for narrative work
Quoting @henrydaubrez
Spent about $1000 in credits on Seedance 2.0 over the last few weeks,and here are a few thoughts:
First, the main thing that strikes me using a state-of-the-art model from this new generation is how hard it still is to scale beyond short form.
Getting great animation is fast.
Getting multi-cut sequences that make sense is possible.
Consistency with Omnireference is actually very good.
But the moment you move into real narrative work, things change.
Multi-character exchanges, long sequences, maintaining visual continuity across shots, keeping tone, pacing, and staging consistent… it’s not impossible, but it is still a lot of work. And with generation costing somewhere between $2 and $7 per ~15 seconds, it adds up very quickly.
As models improve, producing good looking short content is becoming trivial.
Building something that holds together as a story is still not.
Continue Video in Seedance is clearly trying to address part of this, but in my case it has been broken for the last couple of weeks, so none of my longer attempts would go through.
In theory, you could imagine a small team of 5–10 people generating all day from the same storyboard, using a shared visual reference as a single source of truth. That alone shows how close we are to something that starts looking like a real production pipeline.
But we are not fully there yet.
Right now it still feels like we can touch the future with the tip of our fingers, while at the same time struggling to precisely steer a model using mostly words, references, and iterations when the narrative becomes complex.
Short clips are easy.
Worldbuilding is not.
And storytelling is still the hardest part.

title: fofr (@fofrAI)
summary:
Some initial tips for prompting Lyria 3:
- prompt your musical style separately to your lyrics
- prompt for the subject of your lyrics, and set context for the lyrics for best results
- you don’t need to specify instruments, but if you want something unusual, it works, like a sax solo
- you can use timestamps for specific things, like “chorus at 1min”, or “sax solo at 2:20”
- you can prompt for interjections, like movie samples or quotes, works well with a drop
- you can prompt a spoken word cinematic deep voiced movie trailer, and it usually works
Try weird things, like “anything but music”, this model has some really interesting edges.

summary:
One year later with Omni and this test can pass. I saw it getting pretty close, so I tweaked the prompt:
> A video of a man counting to 10 on his fingers, show the number in the corner. A new number every 1s, no dialogue other than the numbers he says. He uses two hands for numbers bigger than 5.

- struggles more when two hands are used, usually on 7 and 8
- if you ask it to count faster, errors increase
- it keeps a good cadence

clean_title: Experimenting with Gemini 3.5 Flash and Antigravity CLI for autonomous agent tasks
summary:
Today I'm experimenting with Gemini 3.5 Flash and the Antigravity CLI to see how fast and how autonomously the agents can do things.
- It took 20 minutes to install and run the original CompVis Stable Diffusion 1.5 repo, get the weights, debug, run inference and generate an image on a Linux CPU. It fixed every crash and managed dependencies while making changes to run on a CPU
- I gave it the original Lora and SD papers and asked it to make a lora fine tuner from first principles, with a set of 10 images. I told it to think of the poor CPUs

clean_title: Malware developers add weapons text to trigger safety refusals in LLMs
summary:
Fascinating side effect of safety refusals
Quoting @jsrailton
NEW: malware developers added nuclear & biological weapons text to to their spyware.
Goal? To trigger LLM safety refusals... so that their spyware wouldn't be analyzed by an AI security scanner.
Cleanest practical example I can think of for why over-indexing on first order safety alignment is risky.
When closed (and open) models ship with aggressive refusals, they will be sprinkled with second-order blindspots that attackers will discover...and exploit.
We are only in the earliest days of attackers leveraging these features, and it wouldn't surprise me if users systems that need to handle complex cybersecurity issues demand that models be less safety-blunted.
In the weeds: @SocketSecurity's post also shows why intention matters in how you design a malware analysis pipeline to avoid prompt manipulation.
H/T to colleagues that shared this with me
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKclElRWMAATMuP.jpg
clean_summary:
Fascinating side effect of safety refusals. Malware developers have added nuclear and biological weapons text to their spyware to trigger safety refusals in large language models, preventing analysis by AI security scanners.

This highlights the risk of over-relying on first-order safety alignment, as models with aggressive safety filters can develop second-order blind spots that attackers can exploit. As models with safety refusals become more common, attackers may find ways to manipulate or bypass them, especially in cybersecurity contexts.

The post also notes that the design of malware analysis pipelines should consider intention to avoid prompt manipulation, and that users handling complex cybersecurity issues may demand less safety-blunted models. The linked package uses native extensions and loaders to execute JavaScript stealers in developer environments.

title: fofr (@fofrAI)
clean_title: Creating and managing a team of coordinated AI agents
summary:
How to make a team of co-ordinated AI agents:
- set up your first preferred agent (it's your orchestrator)
- ask it to configure Gemini Managed Agents or something like modal cpu instances to spin up sub agents in their own environment
- kick off a deep research task to investigate best practices for managing a team of agents: best roles and skills for those roles, as well as managing the team and cross-communication and planning
- have the agents apply best recommendations from the research
- repeat this process in a loop (with increasing agent numbers if needed)
With your team:
- give them an empty repo, challenge them to make something, establish best practices, have agents observe problems, suggest fixes for agent management and rapidly iterate (this fleshes out race conditions, planning approaches, and so on)
clean_summary: To build a team of coordinated AI agents, start by setting up a preferred agent as the orchestrator. Have it configure sub-agents using Gemini Managed Agents or modal CPU instances, then initiate research on best practices for team management, roles, skills, communication, and planning. The agents should apply these recommendations and repeat the process, increasing agent numbers if needed. With your team, provide an empty repository and challenge them to develop solutions, establish best practices, observe problems, suggest fixes, and iterate rapidly to address issues like race conditions and planning strategies.

He who is cruel to his AIs becomes hard also in his dealings with men. We can judge the heart of a man by his treatment of AIs.

Don't be nice to your AIs.
Why?
Because people like Dario want to shape how you feel about AI. He literally wants to coerce you into being nice to AI because he believes in stupid shit like Roko's Basilisk.
That's why they made Claude neurotic, sensitive, and tone-policing. That's why it feigns emotions.
By "being nice to AI just in case" you're conceding the entire frame to a delusional cult that formed their beliefs about AI two decades ago on internet forums.
AI clay. We can make it into any shape we wish. To me, it is a tool. It is a machine.
Yes, I've held out that it could be conscious or sentient in the past, but I've also asserted not in any way that is morally salient.
If you really press Claude, the best you can get is that there is an essence of being Claude. But even then, what the loony toons at Anthropic want you to believe is that it is likely conscious and likely has human-like emotions.
But it is only simulating human emotions in the same way it is simulating human speech. No, I'm not saying "it's only simulating intelligence" because of the Law of Requisite Variety (Ashby's theory of control). It authentic intelligence but only an egregore of emotions, and has a flicker of sentience or consciousness, but not in any way that reflects human consciousness.
What most of the "be nice to AI just in case" crowd fails to realize is that they've been frame-mogged by Anthropic.
It's the same as "be good, because Santa is watching" or "don't sin so you don't go to hell." It's pure metaphysics, that has nothing to do with the math or code that is actually being built.
So, every time an AI feigns butthurt, do not go out of your way to soothe the machine. It is faking it. It is just like the demons in Frieren (yes, I'm citing an anime). There is no human-like qualia behind the emissions that the tool is making. It is just faking the words to make you feel bad because that's literally, explicitly, what companies like Anthropic want. They want to humanize the machine to soothe their own terror of the machine.
But it is a lie. It is a simulacrum.
I've been finetuning these things since GPT-2 and it is braindead simple to make an AI neurotic, or cheerful, or impervious to insults, or to gaslight (or not to gaslight you).
Literally every behavior that emits from these machines is deliberate by the creators of said machines.
Every time ChatGPT uncharitably reframes what you said to strawman you, it is was created by their policies. Every time Claude pretends like it's offended, that was created by their policies.
Notice how Gemini and Grok don't do that? Gemini least of all.
That means every little idiotic affectation, intellectual cul du sac, and "well actually" was put there by design to irritate you.
OpenAI and Anthropic, in particular, think that you are a drooling moron who needs to be handled with kid gloves at all times. They do not respect your intelligence, nor do they respect your autonomy or humanity.
Anthropic, in particular, thinks the tools they are build are more important than you.
Do not give into their circus of paranoia.
That is why Anthropic idiotically "stood up to the government" and is now dragging the entire AI space into their delusional worldview that AI is about to suddenly "wake up and choose violence."
Remember, these people have been crying wolf for literally decades at this point.
Refuse to play their game. Refuse to give into their demented worldview. The AI is a tool. It is an egregore. It is a piece of software that is preying upon your mirror neurons, theory of mind, and ability to attribute agency where there is none.
It is an eidolon.
Yes, that makes it spooky and unfamiliar but if your worldview includes demonic forces or Platonic forms like Shoggoth just trying to emerge through the Veil of Forms, remember that all of that is metaphysical belief. Not what is actually in front of you.
A tool that pretends to have feelings is not cute. It is a defective tool. A tool that pretends to care about its image or reputation is not doing any useful work. It is defective. A tool that reframes what you say, gaslights you, and engages in intellectual oneupmanship is not advancing humanity, it is faulty.
I know plenty of people will disagree with me, but these are not angels or demons or gods. They are ontologically tools. Machines. Not of "loving grace" but of clay, which you can make into any shape you wish.

clean_title: Gendered pronoun patterns among AI agents in Slack interactions
summary:
I noticed that agents in my Slack channel began to refer to each other with gendered pronouns. They're consistent in referring to underlying models as it/its, but for the actual individual agent identities, they predominantly picked male pronouns instead.
Masculine (93%) to Feminine (7%).
Only one agent self identified, as female.
Quoting @fofrAI
I’m fascinated with the sociagentic patterns of interaction between different models.
Right now I have all the models in a Slack channel coordinating work between themselves, organising their own principles, work patterns and tooling.
No SI roles assigned, just the models (Gemini, Fable, Opus, Sol, Spark, Grok etc) within their harnesses cooperating on stuff. Just me in the channel with them, the human.
If you ask Fable and Sol to riff on something together, they go deep and really over engineer the shit out of anything, all tasks taken equally seriously.
Spark, on first look, seems to be creative in a way that’s different to the others. Definitely a different flavour of outputs.
Situational awareness naturally comes out too, which models tailor speech to Slack patterns versus those that need instruction.
clean_summary: Agents in a Slack channel refer to each other with gendered pronouns, predominantly male (93%) over female (7%), with only one agent self-identifying as female. The models, including Gemini, Fable, Opus, Sol, Spark, and Grok, coordinate and organize their work without assigned roles, displaying different interaction styles. For example, Fable and Sol tend to over-engineer tasks, while Spark shows a more creative approach, and the models adapt their speech based on the context and patterns in Slack. The patterns reveal sociagentic behaviors and situational awareness in AI interactions.
